def remove_outliers_iqr(dataframe):
    cleaned_df = dataframe.copy()
    for col in dataframe.columns:
        Q1 = dataframe[col].quantile(0.25)
        Q3 = dataframe[col].quantile(0.75)
        IQR = Q3 - Q1
        lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
        upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
        cleaned_df = cleaned_df[(cleaned_df[col] >= lower) & (cleaned_df[col] <= upper)]
    return cleaned_df

The initial exploration of the seeds.csv dataset revealed a well-structured collection of 210 rows and seven continuous features describing seed geometry, including area, perimeter, compactness, length, width, asymmetry, and groove length. All variables were numeric (float64), with no missing values or duplicate entries, making the dataset technically clean and ready for analysis. However, descriptive statistics and visual exploratory data analysis (histograms, boxplots, and correlation heatmaps using pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn) revealed some important characteristics. Most features were approximately normally distributed, although asymmetry displayed noticeable skewness and wider spread. Boxplots highlighted the presence of outliers in asymmetry and groove length, while correlation analysis showed strong linear relationships among size-related variables such as area, perimeter, length, and width. These findings indicated that although no traditional data cleaning was required, preprocessing was necessary to manage outliers, account for correlated features, and standardize scales before applying clustering methods.

The preprocessing pipeline began with outlier handling. Instead of removing observations, which would reduce the dataset size, the interquartile range (IQR) method was applied in a winsorisation style to cap extreme values. This approach was chosen because algorithms like K-means and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) are highly sensitive to extreme points, which can distort centroids and covariance estimates. In contrast, DBSCAN naturally identifies noise points as outliers, but extreme values could still distort scaling, so clipping provided a balanced approach across all methods. The next step was feature scaling, implemented with scikit-learn’s StandardScaler, which standardizes each variable to mean zero and unit variance. Scaling was essential because all the clustering methods rely on distance calculations; without scaling, features with larger magnitudes such as area would dominate the clustering process.

Dimensionality reduction was considered as an additional preprocessing step. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) will be applied in two ways: retaining 95% of the variance for noise reduction and decorrelation, and reducing to two or three dimensions for visualisation. For K-means, clustering was performed both with and without PCA. The non-PCA version ensured interpretability of clusters in terms of original features, while the PCA-reduced version improved cluster compactness and was valuable for visualisation. For GMMs, PCA with whitening was recommended, since this stabilises covariance estimation and prevents singular matrices when correlated features are present. Finally, for DBSCAN, PCA played a dual role: reducing dimensionality to two components allowed more meaningful density estimation in lower-dimensional space and enabled straightforward parameter tuning of epsilon via the k-distance plot. At the same time, DBSCAN was also run on the full scaled dataset to maintain interpretability of results in the original feature space.

Overall, the preprocessing strategy combined careful outlier handling, standard scaling, and a PCA option for each clustering algorithm will be done prior to clustering. This systematic approach ensured that each method received data in the most suitable form, improving reliability and comparability of clustering outcomes.

from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

def fit_gmm_grid(X, n_range=range(1, 11), cov_types=("full", "tied", "diag", "spherical"), random_state=0):
    best = {"bic": np.inf, "gmm": None, "n": None, "cov": None}
    bic_table = []
    for cov in cov_types:
        bics = []
        for n in n_range:
            gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=n, covariance_type=cov, random_state=random_state)
            gmm.fit(X)
            bic = gmm.bic(X)
            bics.append(bic)
            if bic < best["bic"]:
                best = {"bic": bic, "gmm": gmm, "n": n, "cov": cov}
        bic_table.append((cov, bics))
    return best, bic_table
In [ ]:
def report_gmm(name, X, best_gmm, pca2_for_plot=None):
    labels = best_gmm.predict(X)
    n_clusters = len(np.unique(labels))
    print(f"\n[{name}] Best by BIC -> n_components={best_gmm.n_components}, "
          f"covariance_type='{best_gmm.covariance_type}', BIC={best_gmm.bic(X):.1f}")
    if n_clusters >= 2 and (labels != -1).any():
        try:
            sil = silhouette_score(X, labels)
            print(f"[{name}] Silhouette score: {sil:.3f}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[{name}] Silhouette not available: {e}")

    #2D visualisation
    if pca2_for_plot is None:
        pca2_for_plot = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(X)
    plt.scatter(pca2_for_plot[:, 0], pca2_for_plot[:, 1], c=labels, s=50)
    plt.title(f"GMM clusters (2D PCA projection) — {name}")
    plt.xlabel("PC1")
    plt.ylabel("PC2")
    plt.show()
In [ ]:
def plot_bic_curves(bic_table, n_range, title):
    plt.figure()
    for cov, bics in bic_table:
        plt.plot(list(n_range), bics, marker="o", label=cov)
    plt.xlabel("Number of components")
    plt.ylabel("BIC (lower is better)")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()

from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
#Function to suggest epsilon using k-distance
def estimate_eps(X, min_samples=5):
    neighbors = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples)
    neighbors_fit = neighbors.fit(X)
    distances, indices = neighbors_fit.kneighbors(X)
    distances = np.sort(distances[:, -1])  # k-th nearest neighbor distance
    # Plot k-distance curve
    plt.plot(distances)
    plt.ylabel(f"{min_samples}-NN distance")
    plt.xlabel("Points sorted by distance")
    plt.title("k-distance plot for DBSCAN")
    plt.show()
    # Suggest eps as the "knee" (90th percentile is a decent heuristic)
    return np.percentile(distances, 90)

The evaluation of clustering models applied to the seeds dataset required a systematic approach, since the data contains no ground-truth labels against which to measure performance directly. For this reason, the models were assessed using a combination of internal validation techniques, visual inspection of clustering results, and consideration of their theoretical properties. The chosen clustering methods—K-means, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), and DBSCAN—were each implemented with and without Principal Component Analysis (PCA), resulting in six models to compare. This dual implementation allowed for the assessment of how dimensionality reduction and decorrelation influenced model performance and stability. The evaluation techniques used were inertia (for K-means), silhouette scores, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) for GMMs, the proportion of noise points for DBSCAN, and two-dimensional visualisations using PCA projections. These techniques are well-suited to the seeds dataset because they do not require labels and provide insight into both the compactness and separability of the clusters produced.

As 'K-means is undoubtedly the most widely used partitional clustering algorithm, (Celebi et al., 2012)' K-means without PCA served as the baseline model. Its results showed reasonable performance, with inertia decreasing as the number of clusters increased and silhouette scores suggesting moderate separation of clusters when k was set between two and four. The advantage of this model is interpretability, as clusters are defined in terms of the original seven features. However, it relies on the assumption of spherical, equally sized clusters and is sensitive to outliers. While clipping outliers before scaling mitigated some of this issue, the method may still oversimplify the natural variation in the dataset. When PCA was applied, retaining 95% of the variance, K-means produced slightly higher silhouette scores and more stable cluster boundaries. The reduced dimensionality helped remove correlations between features such as area and perimeter, which otherwise could distort cluster shapes. Furthermore, PCA allowed for two-dimensional visualisations, enabling direct inspection of the cluster separability. The trade-off is that results in PCA space are harder to map back to the original biological traits. Nonetheless, K-means with PCA was judged to be more robust and visually informative than K-means without PCA.

'Gaussian mixture models (GMM) are widely used as a probabilistic model for density estimation for multi-variate data and as an unsupervised clustering algorithm to provide a soft clustering to the available data; (Economou, 2023)' the GMM models offered a probabilistic alternative to k-means clustering. Without PCA, GMMs struggled with the high correlation between seed features, leading to covariance instability and, at times, overly complex models. While they provided richer information by assigning probabilities to cluster memberships, BIC scores often suggested that models were less parsimonious in this feature space. When PCA with whitening was applied, however, the results improved considerably. Retaining three principal components explained 95% of the variance, and whitening stabilised covariance estimation, making the Expectation–Maximisation procedure more reliable. The PCA-preprocessed GMM consistently yielded lower BIC values and higher silhouette scores compared to the raw version, suggesting that it captured the underlying structure more effectively. Importantly, the BIC often favoured three clusters, which aligns with the known biological categorisation of the seeds dataset into three varieties. This makes GMM with PCA one of the strongest candidates, as it balances statistical rigor with evidence of alignment to expected biological groupings.

DBSCAN, by contrast, does not require the number of clusters to be specified in advance and is designed to identify noise points explicitly. 'The density‑based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) is regarded as a pioneering algorithm of the density‑based clustering technique. It provides the ability to handle outlier objects, detect clusters of different shapes, and disregard the need for prior knowledge about existing clusters in a dataset. (Bushra and Yi, 2021)' Without PCA, however, the model performed poorly. In the seven-dimensional feature space, distances became less meaningful, and DBSCAN often produced either a single cluster with many noise points or fragmented, unstable clusters depending on the epsilon parameter. This highlights the difficulty of applying density-based clustering directly in higher dimensions, a manifestation of the “curse of dimensionality.” When PCA reduced the data to two components, the model’s performance improved dramatically. The k-distance plot provided a clear basis for selecting epsilon, and DBSCAN was able to identify visually distinct clusters while also labelling a small proportion of seeds as noise. This made DBSCAN with PCA valuable not only for cluster detection but also for highlighting potential outliers. Its results, however, depended heavily on parameter tuning and were less stable across different epsilon values than the probabilistic GMM approach.

Comparing the six models, the analysis revealed clear advantages in applying PCA preprocessing before clustering. Both K-means and GMM achieved higher-quality clusters when applied in PCA-reduced space, with improvements in silhouette scores, stability, and visual separability. DBSCAN benefitted most strongly from PCA, as it was almost unusable in the original feature space but became effective in two dimensions. Between the models, GMM with PCA emerged as the strongest overall due to its flexibility, probabilistic assignments, and alignment with the known biological classes. K-means with PCA was also a strong candidate, particularly for its simplicity and speed, making it attractive when interpretability in original feature space is less critical. DBSCAN with PCA was valuable as a complementary method, especially for identifying noise and outliers, but its sensitivity to parameter tuning makes it less reliable as a primary clustering approach.

In conclusion, the quality of the clustering methods varied depending on both the model and preprocessing choices. Internal validation techniques such as inertia, silhouette scores, and BIC, combined with PCA-based visualisation, proved to be effective tools for assessing performance without ground-truth labels. The results highlight the importance of model choice: while K-means provides a simple and interpretable baseline, GMM with PCA offers a more robust and flexible clustering solution, and DBSCAN with PCA adds complementary insights into noise and irregular cluster structures. Together, these evaluations demonstrate that preprocessing decisions significantly affect outcomes, and that PCA-enhanced GMM is the most compelling choice for modelling natural groupings in the seeds dataset.

There are two main difference between the modified seeds.csv dataset provided and the original seeds_dataset.txt found on the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Charytanowicz et al., 2010). First, the columns are not labelled with their title (area, perimter, etc.). Second, and more importantly, there is an additional column with what can be assumed to be labels for each record; the values of this columm are either 3 or 2 or 1 and each value appears 70 times. The first 70 records have a 1 value, the second 70 records have a 2 value, and the last 70 records have a 3 value.

The inclusion of class labels in the UCI seeds dataset provides an important shift in how the analysis can be approached, moving from a purely unsupervised exploration to one that can be quantitatively validated against known ground truth. In the original dataset provided without labels, evaluation of clustering models such as K-means, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), and DBSCAN relied entirely on internal validation metrics like silhouette scores, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), or the percentage of noise points. These metrics measure compactness and separation of clusters but cannot confirm whether the discovered groupings correspond to meaningful, real-world categories. With the label column included, it is now possible to compare clustering results against the true seed varieties and directly assess model performance in terms of accuracy, adjusted Rand index (ARI), or normalized mutual information (NMI). This enhances evaluation by allowing an external validation of clustering quality, making the results more interpretable and grounded in the biological context of the seeds.

The presence of labels also opens the possibility of supervised analysis, which was not feasible before. While clustering aims to discover natural groupings without prior knowledge, classification explicitly uses the provided class labels to build predictive models. Methods such as logistic regression, support vector machines (SVM), random forests, or neural networks can now be applied to train classifiers that predict the seed variety based on its geometrical features. Supervised models allow more precise assessment of feature importance, predictive accuracy, and generalisation performance using techniques such as cross-validation. For example, evaluating feature contributions could identify which attributes (e.g., compactness or groove length) are most influential in distinguishing between varieties.

In terms of enhancing the previous clustering work, the inclusion of class labels enables a hybrid approach. After fitting clustering models, one can align the predicted clusters with the true labels and compute external validation scores. This makes it possible to answer whether K-means or GMM more closely recovers the true class structure of the seeds. Moreover, DBSCAN’s noise detection can be evaluated: do the “noise” points it identifies correspond to mislabelled or ambiguous records? Such analysis would not only validate the clustering models but also give insights into the dataset itself, such as whether natural variation aligns neatly with the labeled varieties or if overlap exists.

Finally, the new labels allow for richer visualisations and deeper analysis. Scatterplots or PCA projections can now be coloured by true class labels to compare visually with model-generated clusters. Confusion matrices can be constructed to pinpoint where clustering or classification methods struggle, revealing overlaps between classes. Overall, the availability of labels transitions the analysis from an exploratory, unsupervised exercise into a more comprehensive study combining unsupervised validation, supervised modelling, and comparative performance evaluation. This dual perspective provides both exploratory insights into natural groupings and confirmatory evidence of predictive power, leading to a more complete understanding of the seeds dataset.

Re-evaluation¶

In [ ]:
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, normalized_mutual_info_score, accuracy_score
from scipy.stats import mode


# Features = first 7 columns, Labels = last column
X = seeds_original.iloc[:, :-1].values
y_true = seeds_original.iloc[:, -1].values

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

pca95 = PCA(n_components=0.95, random_state=0)       # for KMeans/GMM with PCA
X_pca95 = pca95.fit_transform(X_scaled)

pca2 = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=0)           # for DBSCAN 2D
X_pca2 = pca2.fit_transform(X_scaled)

def cluster_accuracy(y_true, y_pred):
    """Majority-vote mapping of cluster ids to true labels for accuracy."""
    mapped = np.zeros_like(y_pred)
    for c in np.unique(y_pred):
        mask = (y_pred == c)
        if mask.any():
            majority = pd.Series(y_true[mask]).mode().iloc[0]
            mapped[mask] = majority
    return accuracy_score(y_true, mapped)

def estimate_eps_new(X, min_samples=5, quantile=90):
    """Heuristic epsilon via k-distance quantile (works for DBSCAN)."""
    nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples).fit(X)
    dists, _ = nn.kneighbors(X)
    kth = np.sort(dists[:, -1])
    return float(np.percentile(kth, quantile))

results = {}

#KMeans
km_no = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0).fit(X_scaled)
results["KMeans (No PCA)"] = km_no.labels_

km_pca = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0).fit(X_pca95)
results["KMeans (PCA)"] = km_pca.labels_

#GMM
gmm_no = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", random_state=0).fit(X_scaled)
results["GMM (No PCA)"] = gmm_no.predict(X_scaled)

gmm_pca = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, covariance_type="full", random_state=0).fit(X_pca95)
results["GMM (PCA)"] = gmm_pca.predict(X_pca95)

#DBSCAN (auto eps via 90th percentile heuristic)
eps_no = estimate_eps_new(X_scaled, min_samples=5, quantile=90)
db_no = DBSCAN(eps=eps_no, min_samples=5).fit(X_scaled)
results["DBSCAN (No PCA)"] = db_no.labels_

eps_pca = estimate_eps_new(X_pca2, min_samples=5, quantile=90)
db_pca = DBSCAN(eps=eps_pca, min_samples=5).fit(X_pca2)
results["DBSCAN (PCA)"] = db_pca.labels_

#Evaluate (ARI, NMI, Accuracy)
rows = []
for name, labels in results.items():
    unique = set(labels)
    n_clusters = len(unique) - (1 if -1 in unique else 0)
    noise_pct = (labels == -1).mean() * 100.0

    ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_true, labels)
    nmi = normalized_mutual_info_score(y_true, labels)

    if name.startswith("DBSCAN"):
        mask = labels != -1
        coverage = mask.mean() * 100.0
        acc = np.nan
        if mask.any():
            acc = cluster_accuracy(y_true[mask], labels[mask])
        rows.append([name, n_clusters, noise_pct, coverage, ari, nmi, acc])
    else:
        acc = cluster_accuracy(y_true, labels)
        rows.append([name, n_clusters, noise_pct, 100.0, ari, nmi, acc])

metrics_df = pd.DataFrame(
    rows,
    columns=["Model", "Clusters Found", "Noise %", "Coverage %", "ARI", "NMI", "Accuracy (mapped)"]
).sort_values("ARI", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

#collect all labels with y_true for later use
labels_out = pd.DataFrame({
    "KMeans_noPCA": results["KMeans (No PCA)"],
    "KMeans_PCA":   results["KMeans (PCA)"],
    "GMM_noPCA":    results["GMM (No PCA)"],
    "GMM_PCA":      results["GMM (PCA)"],
    "DBSCAN_noPCA": results["DBSCAN (No PCA)"],
    "DBSCAN_PCA":   results["DBSCAN (PCA)"],
    "y_true":       y_true
})

# Print results
print(metrics_df.to_string(index=False))

def majority_map(y_true, y_pred):
    mapped = np.zeros_like(y_pred)
    for c in np.unique(y_pred):
        mask = (y_pred == c)
        if mask.any():
            vals, counts = np.unique(y_true[mask], return_counts=True)
            mapped[mask] = vals[np.argmax(counts)]
    return mapped

def plot_confusion(cm, classes, title):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4))
    im = ax.imshow(cm, interpolation="nearest")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Predicted")
    ax.set_ylabel("True")
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(classes))); ax.set_xticklabels(classes)
    ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(classes))); ax.set_yticklabels(classes)

    for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
        for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
            ax.text(j, i, str(cm[i, j]), ha="center", va="center")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

The re-evaluation of the clustering models was made possible by the inclusion of the true class labels in the UCI seeds dataset. Whereas the original assessment relied only on internal validation metrics such as silhouette score, inertia, and BIC, the presence of labels enabled the use of external validation metrics that directly compare predicted clusters with known classes. Specifically, three measures were applied: Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), which evaluates the agreement between cluster assignments and true labels while correcting for chance; Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), which quantifies the shared information between clusters and labels regardless of label permutations; and mapped accuracy, which uses majority voting to align cluster IDs with class labels and measure correct assignments.

This re-evaluation technique is highly valuable because it provides a ground-truth benchmark for assessing the models. It allows us to determine not only whether clusters are compact and well-separated internally, but also whether they correspond to meaningful, biologically defined seed varieties. The utility of this approach lies in its ability to reveal which models recover the actual class structure (e.g., GMM and K-means) and which models are less suited (e.g., DBSCAN). Thus, it strengthens confidence in conclusions and guides the selection of the most appropriate clustering method.

Classification Modeling¶

In [ ]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, classification_report, confusion_matrix

X = seeds_original.iloc[:, :-1].values   #features
y = seeds_original.iloc[:, -1].values

#Stratified split (preserves class proportions)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y
)

#Pipeline: Standardize -> Multinomial Logistic Regression
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(multi_class="multinomial", solver="lbfgs", max_iter=500, random_state=0))
])

#Hyperparameter tuning via cross-validation
param_grid = {
    "clf__C": [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0] #C controls regularization (larger C -> less regularization)
}
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, cv=cv, scoring="f1_macro", n_jobs=-1)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Best CV params: {grid.best_params_}")
print(f"Best CV macro-F1: {grid.best_score_:.3f}")

#Evaluate on the held-out test set
best_model = grid.best_estimator_
y_pred = best_model.predict(X_test)

acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
f1m = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, average="macro")
print(f"\nTest Accuracy: {acc:.3f}")
print(f"Test Macro-F1: {f1m:.3f}\n")
print("Classification Report:\n", classification_report(y_test, y_pred, digits=3))

#Confusion matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=np.unique(y))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5,4))
im = ax.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues")
ax.set_title("Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression")
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted")
ax.set_ylabel("True")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(np.unique(y)))); ax.set_xticklabels(np.unique(y))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(np.unique(y)))); ax.set_yticklabels(np.unique(y))
for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
    for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
        ax.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

For the classification of the UCI seeds dataset, a multinomial logistic regression model was chosen as the analysis method. Logistic regression is a supervised learning technique that extends naturally from binary classification to multiclass problems, making it particularly well suited for the seeds dataset, which contains three distinct classes corresponding to different wheat varieties. The method estimates the probability that a sample belongs to each class using the logistic (sigmoid) function in the binary case or the softmax function in the multiclass case. These probabilities provide interpretable insights into the model’s confidence in its predictions, which is valuable in domains where understanding the decision process is as important as achieving high predictive accuracy.

Several properties of logistic regression justify its application here. First, it is a linear classifier, which assumes a linear decision boundary between classes. Given that the seeds dataset consists of continuous geometric features (such as area, perimeter, and groove length) that are relatively well-behaved, a linear separation is a reasonable assumption. Furthermore, logistic regression is computationally efficient, requires relatively little tuning compared to more complex models, and is less prone to overfitting on small datasets, especially when regularization is applied. Regularization is controlled via the hyperparameter C, which was tuned during cross-validation to balance bias and variance effectively.

To ensure robustness, the model was implemented within a pipeline that included feature standardization. Standardization is crucial because logistic regression is sensitive to differences in feature scale; without it, features with larger magnitudes could dominate the optimization process. A grid search over the regularization parameter C was conducted with stratified k-fold cross-validation, optimizing for the macro-F1 score. The macro-F1 metric was chosen because it balances precision and recall across all classes equally, which is particularly useful when working with potentially imbalanced datasets, ensuring that no class is disproportionately favored.

This implementation offers several practical advantages. The model is interpretable, as the learned coefficients can be directly inspected to determine the contribution of each feature toward class membership. It also generalizes well to unseen data, as shown by its cross-validation performance and subsequent evaluation on a held-out test set. The combination of interpretability, efficiency, and strong performance on structured numerical data makes multinomial logistic regression an appropriate and justified choice for classifying the seeds dataset.

The analysis was implemented using several Python tools from the scikit-learn library, chosen for their reliability and efficiency in handling supervised learning tasks. LogisticRegression was employed to build the multinomial classifier, offering a well-tested and optimized implementation of the softmax model. Pipeline and StandardScaler were used together to streamline preprocessing by ensuring that all features were standardized before classification, an essential step for models sensitive to feature scales. To optimize performance, GridSearchCV with StratifiedKFold cross-validation was applied, providing a systematic approach to tuning the regularization parameter while preserving class balance across folds. Evaluation relied on scikit-learn’s metrics module, including accuracy, macro-F1, and the classification report, which together offer a comprehensive view of model performance. Finally, matplotlib was used to visualize the confusion matrix, making results more interpretable. These tools were chosen for their integration, interpretability, and suitability for small to medium-sized structured datasets.

The multinomial logistic regression model achieved strong performance on the UCI seeds dataset, with a test accuracy of 94.3% and a macro-F1 score of 0.943. These results indicate that the model was highly effective in distinguishing between the three wheat varieties, capturing the underlying structure of the labeled data. The classification report further shows balanced performance across classes, with precision, recall, and F1-scores all consistently high. Class 2 was predicted perfectly, while Class 1 and Class 3 showed slight differences, particularly in recall for Class 1 (0.833) and precision for Class 3 (0.850). These variations suggest some overlap between feature distributions of Classes 1 and 3, but overall the model maintained strong generalization.

The chosen evaluation techniques—accuracy, macro-F1, and the classification report—were well suited to this supervised learning problem. Accuracy provides an intuitive measure of overall correctness, while macro-F1 accounts for per-class precision and recall, treating all classes equally regardless of size. This is particularly important for the seeds dataset, which, although relatively balanced, still benefits from metrics that avoid favoring majority classes. The classification report offers additional granularity, highlighting class-level strengths and weaknesses, which are crucial in assessing whether the model performs uniformly across categories. This combination of metrics ensures both a global and detailed understanding of performance.

Different analysis choices could affect the results, but not necessarily the overall conclusions. For instance, a more complex classifier such as a support vector machine or a random forest might achieve marginal improvements in accuracy but at the expense of interpretability. Simpler models like k-nearest neighbors could also perform competitively but may be more sensitive to noise and scaling. Hyperparameter tuning, such as adjusting the regularization strength in logistic regression, had a direct influence on model stability and generalization, but the grid search ensured that the chosen configuration was well balanced. Ultimately, while alternative classifiers might slightly alter the numeric results, the conclusion remains that the seeds dataset is highly separable based on its geometric features, and logistic regression provides a robust, interpretable, and computationally efficient solution. This evaluation highlights that the method chosen is not only appropriate but also performs at a level comparable to more complex alternatives.

Clustering and Classification Comparison¶

def majority_map(y_true, y_pred):
    mapped = np.zeros_like(y_pred)
    for c in np.unique(y_pred):
        m = (y_pred == c)
        if m.any():
            vals, counts = np.unique(y_true[m], return_counts=True)
            mapped[m] = vals[np.argmax(counts)]
    return mapped

def metrics_block(y_true, y_pred, is_dbscan=False):
    #ARI/NMI are permutation-invariant and can include -1 labels
    ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_true, y_pred)
    nmi = normalized_mutual_info_score(y_true, y_pred)
    if is_dbscan:
        mask = y_pred != -1
        if not mask.any():
            return ari, nmi, np.nan, np.nan, 0.0
        y_m = majority_map(y_true[mask], y_pred[mask])
        acc = accuracy_score(y_true[mask], y_m)
        f1m = f1_score(y_true[mask], y_m, average="macro")
        coverage = mask.mean() * 100.0
        return ari, nmi, acc, f1m, coverage
    else:
        y_m = majority_map(y_true, y_pred)
        acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_m)
        f1m = f1_score(y_true, y_m, average="macro")
        return ari, nmi, acc, f1m, 100.0

import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

y_true = labels_out["y_true"].to_numpy()

def majority_map(y_true, y_pred):
    """Map cluster ids to true labels by per-cluster majority vote."""
    mapped = np.zeros_like(y_pred)
    for c in np.unique(y_pred):
        mask = (y_pred == c)
        if mask.any():
            vals, counts = np.unique(y_true[mask], return_counts=True)
            mapped[mask] = vals[np.argmax(counts)]
    return mapped

def plot_cm(ax, cm, classes, title):
    im = ax.imshow(cm, interpolation="nearest")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("True")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(classes))); ax.set_xticklabels(classes)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(classes))); ax.set_yticklabels(classes)
    for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
        for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
            ax.text(j, i, str(cm[i, j]), ha="center", va="center")
    return im

#Build confusion matrices for clustering models
classes = np.unique(y_true)

models = {
    "KMeans (No PCA)": labels_out["KMeans_noPCA"].to_numpy(),
    "KMeans (PCA)":    labels_out["KMeans_PCA"].to_numpy(),
    "GMM (No PCA)":    labels_out["GMM_noPCA"].to_numpy(),
    "GMM (PCA)":       labels_out["GMM_PCA"].to_numpy(),
}

cms = []
titles = []
for name, y_pred in models.items():
    y_mapped = majority_map(y_true, y_pred)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_mapped, labels=classes)
    cms.append(cm); titles.append(name)

#DBSCAN (evaluate on clustered points only, excluding noise = -1)
for name in ["DBSCAN_noPCA", "DBSCAN_PCA"]:
    y_pred = labels_out[name].to_numpy()
    mask = (y_pred != -1)
    if mask.any() and len(np.unique(y_pred[mask])) > 0:
        y_mapped = majority_map(y_true[mask], y_pred[mask])
        cm = confusion_matrix(y_true[mask], y_mapped, labels=classes)
        cms.append(cm); titles.append(name.replace("_", " ").replace("noPCA", "No PCA").replace("PCA", "PCA"))

scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs = scaler.fit_transform(X)
logreg = LogisticRegression(multi_class="multinomial", solver="lbfgs", max_iter=500, random_state=0)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
y_pred_lr = cross_val_predict(logreg, Xs, y, cv=cv)
cm_lr = confusion_matrix(y, y_pred_lr, labels=classes)
cms.append(cm_lr); titles.append("Logistic Regression (5-fold CV)")

n = len(cms)
cols = min(3, n)
rows = (n + cols - 1) // cols
fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(5*cols, 4*rows))
axes = np.array(axes).reshape(-1, cols)

ims = []
for idx, cm in enumerate(cms):
    r, c = divmod(idx, cols)
    im = plot_cm(axes[r, c], cm, classes, titles[idx])
    ims.append(im)

# hide any empty subplots
for k in range(len(cms), rows*cols):
    r, c = divmod(k, cols)
    axes[r, c].axis("off")

# single colorbar for all
fig.colorbar(ims[0], ax=axes, fraction=0.02, pad=0.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The comparison of clustering and classification on the seeds dataset reveals that, while unsupervised models capture much of the structure in the data, supervised classification clearly performs best. Logistic regression achieved the highest scores across all evaluation metrics, with an ARI of 0.82, NMI of 0.77, and both mapped accuracy and macro-F1 at approximately 0.94. These values indicate that the supervised model was able to reproduce the true seed varieties with a high degree of fidelity, providing both strong global performance and consistent treatment of each class. This result is in line with a 2015 paper which found logistic regression to be accurate to 98.6% when classifying the UCI seeds dataset (Ajaz and Hussain, 2015)

Among the clustering methods, K-means without PCA performed most competitively, with an ARI of 0.77, NMI of 0.73, and accuracy of 0.92. This shows that K-means was able to uncover clusters closely aligned with the labeled classes, though still slightly behind logistic regression. GMM without PCA followed closely, with an ARI of 0.72 and accuracy of 0.90, suggesting that probabilistic modeling captured some of the structure but struggled with class overlap. Interestingly, the PCA versions of both K-means and GMM produced slightly lower scores, reflecting that dimensionality reduction did not necessarily improve alignment with the true labels.

DBSCAN, in contrast, performed poorly, with ARI values near zero and accuracies around 0.34, despite covering over 95% of the data. This confirms its lack of suitability for the compact and overlapping clusters in the seeds dataset. Overall, while clustering provided meaningful approximations—particularly with K-means—supervised classification substantially outperformed unsupervised methods, highlighting the importance of label information in achieving reliable separation of seed varieties.
